Wow, thank you. Googled for this like crazy & searched within PhpStorm & WebStorm and didn't see it for several days. Couldn't put up with the 'almost right' keybindings today though, and finally saw this. SO MUCH BETTER.

Few issues/discrepancies between this keymap & the VS-for-mac defaults -- those quirks as follows:

  • 'Delete' key should be bound to 'delete' (currently only binds CMD+Backspace)
  • "Top of file" = CMD+Up (currently is move block up)
  • "Bottom of file" = CMD+Down (currently is move block down)
  • Tab navigation appears to always conflict with system settings, though I can't find the system settings that are in conflict (CMD+] and CMD+[)
  • Not 100% but I thought CMD+1...5 worked like they do in Chrome, selecting the corresponding tab (not editor drawers/windows).

Note, it's possible they've changed their defaults recently and perhaps my local settings weren't overridden (though I've setup new dev machines recently so I don't think that's the case, but can't say for certain).

Overall, so much better though!. Frankly this should be built-in, probably should replace the "other" VS-for-macOS keymap [or be the default VS-for-mac map, as opposed to the other one, at least].

The other "VS for Mac" keybindings [that are built-in] are likely from before the VS-for-mac codebase was merged with Xamarin's stuff -- they definitely are not bindings I've ever been exposed to, at least, and I've been using MonoDevelop, now VS-for-mac (whatever's bundled with Unity on macOS) for ~10 years now. :)

Thank you!

This plugin has serious bugs:

  1. Every time I add a new string, the content for the main language is discarded (deleted) as soon as I switch to another string. Then, I have to enter the string in the main language a second time to actually save it. This literally happens every single time and is extremely frustrating.

  2. Ctrl-Z changes its behaviour depending on what UI element is focussed. If the text input field is focussed, Ctrl-Z reverts the local changes in that text box. However, if no input field is selected, the i18n key that was added most recently is deleted. This behaviour is quite confusing.

  3. New strings are not always inserted in the correct place (i.e. sorted alphabetically), but are instead appended at the bottom for no apparent reason sometimes.

  4. In “By prefixes” mode, the i18n keys are displayed as a foldable tree. If you click on a non-leaf node (i.e. an i18n key that has children), then the text input fields still show the values of the last (most recently viewed) i18n key. Let's say you have the keys user, user.name and user.email. If you first select user.name and then click on user, you will still see the translations for user.name in the text fields and not those for user. If you want to edit user, you must click on <property> instead. This makes accidental modifications much more likely.

  5. In the list of i18n keys on the left, the currently selected one is not highlighted. In other words, you have to guess which i18n key you're currently editing and hope that it's the right one.

  6. It's much slower than the rest of the IDE's UI.

  7. As far as I can tell, the text input fields don't support linting/highlighting/suggestions by other plugins.

Other than that, the design is bad. You can only see the contents for one i18n key at a time; I would prefer if there were a toggle somewhere. The text input fields have a fixed height (i.e. can't be resized), meaning that editing long texts is a pain. There are also no soft line-breaks.

Tailwind v4 isn't supported out-of-the-box but there's a workaround thankfully. It seems like Jetbrains' Tailwind plugin detects its configuration from the tailwind.config.{ts/js} file. Tailwind v4 has moved away from that format so I imagine this workaround won't work in future versions, but for now it seems like in Tailwind v4 they support the backwards compatible @config directive to load a "legacy" Tailwind config file: tailwindcss.com/docs/functions-and-directives#config-directive

Specifying the configuration in my tailwind.config.ts file and importing it with @config into my CSS file allows IntelliJ to detect the Tailwind config and provide auto-complete suggestions while I can still use v4. So that's my workaround but I imagine it won't work in the next version.

com.itcodebox.fxtools.id.comment: Not bad, not bad. It's very convenient to use and has been a great help to me.

绝对的生产力神器：JavaFX 开发的终极工具箱 作为一名长期从事 JavaFX 开发的工程师，我必须说，JavaFX Tools 是我用过的最强大的插件，它彻底改变了我编写 UI 代码的方式。 在使用这款插件之前，编写 CSS 样式和处理图标往往是一个繁琐且容易出错的过程，需要频繁查阅文档。但自从安装了它，我的开发效率得到了质的飞跃。

  1. 无与伦比的 CSS 智能提示 这是该插件的核心亮点。它提供了 210+ 个 -fx-* 属性的自动补全，并且是“类型感知”的。这意味着当我输入属性值时，IDE 会立刻提示正确的语法。最让我惊喜的是它对第三方库（如 ControlsFX, JFoenix）的自动检测，这让我的项目集成变得非常顺畅。
  2. 图标与 SVG 的完美解决方案 插件内置的 Icon Browser 简直是宝藏。拥有超过 63,000 个图标，我可以直接在 IDE 里搜索、预览，并一键复制 SVG 路径或代码。配合 SVG Path Extractor，处理矢量图形变得前所未有的简单。再也不用在浏览器和代码编辑器之间来回切换了。
  3. 直观的代码辅助 Gutter Previews（侧边栏预览）： 在 CSS 代码旁边直接显示颜色、渐变或图标的预览图，点击还能打开编辑器，这种所见即所得的体验太棒了。 FXML 协助： 自动生成 fx:id、处理资源路径导航以及 i18n 支持，大大减少了样板代码的编写。 属性生成： 通过 Generate 菜单快速生成 JavaFX 属性（包括 CssMetaData），节省了大量重复造轮子的时间。
  4. 稳定且现代化 版本 2.0.0 的重写非常成功，基于 Gradle 8 和 Kotlin DSL，运行流畅且没有 JavaFX 运行时依赖，兼容性极佳。 总结： 如果你正在进行 JavaFX 开发，千万不要错过这款插件。它不仅是一个工具，更像是一个贴心的开发伙伴，让繁琐的 UI 编码变得既高效又愉悦。强烈推荐给每一位 JavaFX 开发者！

Good syntax highlighting, but it repeatedly re-enabled the preview feature itself on startup, when I disabled it before. I don't want the preview, it creates a directory "out" on the root (why?!? do that in a temp dir, don't mess around in my repository), and if you have a huge model or more models in one project, it blocks your whole IDE because it's rendering the preview. It also automatically looks for an OpenSCAD executable without asking, and if it finds one, it sets the path in the plugin settings. So if you remove the path to the executable to prevent rendering, on next startup, it will find the executable again, start rendering, block the IDE, create an out directory, and the loop begins again.

Hi, the plugin doesn't support HTML files, as HTML is already it's own language. The plugin does not support navigating to or from HTML files. I could potentially work on supporting navigating to Keywords defined in HTML files, but it's not in the works. As to .txt files, it should work fine if you associate the plugin with .txt files. However, I would highly recommend renaming all your txt files to .robot, since that way they won't conflict with any files that are .txt, non-robot files in your project. You can find a simple bash script to recursively rename all .txt files in a directory.

If you get version 1.2.3, you might have to "Invalidate caches and restart" from the IntelliJ main menu. Renamed an important class to be a less confusing name, but it's a class that's indexed as a PsiStub, so it causes a console error if you have a stale index. (RobotKeywordDef --> RobotKeywordTitle, since it represents the "title" of a Robot keyword inside a ***Keywords*** table).

Yes, this is possible to associate this plugin with .txt files. If you go to Preferences --> File Types, then look for the entry for my plugin. The entry is called "Text file used by Robot Framework to defined test cases in the Robot DSL". Click the + button, and add "*.txt" as a registered pattern. com.ray.ideaplugin.mybatis-navigator.comment: 这款IDEA插件极大地提升了我的开发效率。首先，它的界面友好，易于上手，特别适合新手使用。插件提供了智能代码补全和实时错误检测，让我能更快地找到并修复问题。此外，集成的文档查看功能使得我在编码时无需频繁切换窗口，节省了很多时间。 值得一提的是，插件的更新频率也很高，开发团队持续根据用户反馈进行改进，这让我对其未来充满期待。不过，在某些特定环境下，插件可能会有轻微的性能问题，希望在后续版本中能得到优化。 总体来说，这款插件是每位开发者的得力助手，强烈推荐给正在寻找提高生产力工具的同事们！

com.raysono.intellij.magnolia.comment: This plugin simplifies, magnolia light development a lot. Before it was a great pain point to switch between the yaml files especially when reusing yaml snippets to minimize duplicate code. Using the plugin during a migration from magnolia 5.7 to 6.2 where we had to rewrite a lot of yaml files to adapt to the new configuration standard, having this was priceless.

com.redhat.devtools.intellij.kubernetes.comment: Especially like that it's very fast, is watching resources and seems to consume little resources. It has less features than the official plugin by Jetbrains but fully does the job for me and is far less clunky.

I found this tool very useful.

It allows you to access pods in your kubernetes cluster and manage all other resources (included custom resources) among other things.

I highly recommend it.
Can it autodetect an OpenShift Local instance?

I installed this plugin as Tekton plugin required this. Honestly, this plugin delayed my work due to "Pull from Cluster" feature. I was developing some demo application and didn't want to sync with cluster's resource - such as uid, creationTimestamp, resourceVersion fields as these are not required demo audiences. I uninstalled this pluign after all.

The above is about the demo app development scenario, but I don't still beleive this feature is requreid for production use. To manage many applications, static yaml file doesn't really work. We would need more smart solutions such as Helm, GitOps. Which means I personally can't see the usecases to sync resources with cluster.

Plugin doesn't seem to add any functionality. Compared to the regular kubernetes plugin which gives me not only syntax highlighting and auto-completion but also the possibility to apply yaml files to the cluster etc. Am I doing something wrong? can't find any configuration that I could change either.

I'm using Pycharm v2021.3.1 on Linux and the plugin v0.3.0.83
With the latest update it requires to have telemetry installed to work. Uninstalled
How to use this plugin ? It is enabled but its not auto-completing. YAML file is also not showing with kubernetes icon (it means plugin is not working)

This plugin has absolutely no settings and does not work for me. So I even does not know what an error or how to fix it.

Team members has same (according to description) plugin in VCS and for themit works perfect

the only thing this plugin seems to provide in pycharm, is listings. You only see the cluster browser on the left, you can list the pods etc. and that's it. No interaction whatsoever, unlike in vscode (where you can follow logs, attach terminal etc.)

com.redhat.devtools.lsp4ij.comment:
LSP4IJ is the reason our BBj language plugin for IntelliJ exists at all. We already had a language server (built with Langium), and LSP4IJ let us bring it to IntelliJ as a first-class citizen — no rewrite of parsing, diagnostics, or completion logic in Java.

Integration was refreshingly simple: declare the server and a language mapping in plugin.xml, implement a small LanguageServerFactory, done. Out of the box our users got diagnostics, code completion, go-to-definition, hover, signature help, and even the Structure View wired to the server's document symbols — all feeling native in the IDE. Where we needed to fine-tune behavior (completion, server lifecycle, status reporting), LSP4IJ's extension points made that straightforward without fighting the framework.

Add to that a very responsive maintainer team and a fast release cadence — for anyone bringing a language server to the JetBrains ecosystem, LSP4IJ is the way to do it.
Great maintainers that actively push this forward.

Very handly tool for bring any language to jetbrains. most of the language now a days have LSP support. It helped me use glsl_analyzer lsp in intellij. i even added new features supported by lsp4ij to glsl_analyzer using codex. Now its feel like home for glsl in the IDE.
Easy to use LSP implementation. This helped me convert the https://github.com/semanticWebLanguageServer/swls to IntelliJ making my colleagues very happy.

It took me only a few days of AI supported work to put this together: https://plugins.jetbrains.com/plugin/31790-nim-using-nimlangserver

Pretty cool!
Great plugin! In the nightly build we're also getting lazy-loading for workspaces and root_markers that will allow easy setup for monorepos even with multiple languages.

I built agnix, a linter for AI agent config files, and LSP4IJ is what made shipping JetBrains support realistic. Writing a native PSI/annotator integration would have been weeks of work for a tool whose validation logic already lives in a Rust LSP server. With LSP4IJ we got diagnostics, quick fixes, hover docs, and a server installer flow working quickly - and the same LSP binary now serves VS Code, Zed, Neovim, and IntelliJ from one codebase.

The server installer flow is especially valuable

users don't need to know what a language server is, it just works. Documentation is solid and UserDefinedLanguageServerSettings covered every case we needed. Thanks to the Red Hat team for maintaining it.
We have used this as a library from our OPA plugin for IDEA, it works great!
I really love this plugin. It really helped me a lot to port my VSCode extension to IntelliJ.

LSP4IJ is an excellent plugin that provides open-source and free LSP support for the IntelliJ IDEA platform, greatly enriching language support and application scenarios. This is particularly important for the Community Edition, and we are very grateful for the contributions of the developers!

LSP4IJ has been essential for building our IntelliJ plugin (intellij-lumos). The framework made it straightforward to integrate our custom LSP server with IntelliJ IDEA and Rust Rover.

The API is well-designed, documentation is clear, and the project is actively maintained. Setting up diagnostics, auto-completion, and hover support was much easier than expected.

If you're building any language support plugin for IntelliJ using LSP, this is the way to go. Highly recommended!

Project: https://github.com/getlumos/intellij-lumos
This is really good extension for integrate another programming languages into single JetBrains IDE. This has a bit problems in some moments, but you can still use that for "stable" developing.

The LSP4IJ plugin provides seamless integration of language servers and debug adapters with a JetBrains IDE. It has its quirks as it needs to be generic enough to support any arbitrary server or adapter but once you get the hang of it it's not so bad. The documentation and screenshots on GitHub are a big help.

The maintainer @angelozerr is very responsive on GitHub and the community around LSP4IJ is just great as I see a lot of back and forth between the two. We're all working together to try to solve the difficult problem of implementing a specification just right so that it will work well for everyone.

Thank you Red Hat for this plugin!
This plugin has helped me tremendously while working on a language server. It does what it was designed to do, and it's pretty easy to use.
Thank you for the plugin, it adds support for debugging in IJ with DebugPy which is great.

com.robohorse.robopojogenerator.comment:
Great plugin, and saves a ton of mundane work when writing clients for third party REST APIs, but I do have a few suggestions for improvement:

  1. It supports almost every third party JSON framework out there, but it doesn't support standard Jakarta EE JSON-B annotations at the moment, which I find a bit interesting. Sure, it's easy enough to replace Jackson @JsonProperty with JSON-B @JsonbProperty and a corresponding import, but it's extra work that really shouldn't be necessary.

  2. It would be nice to choose whether to generate classes for the nested object as inner classes/records (and in my opinion, that should be the default) rather than as top-level classes. At the moment you can easily overwrite classes generated by one JSON by the classes generated by another, even though they may not be the same thing, just because the property names in JSON are the same. Using inner classes/records would eliminate this issue, and after all, it's easy enough to move them to top level in IntelliJ, if so desired.

I think this plugin is very useful but has a lot of room to grow. There's a couple of features I know myself and a lot of others I work with would absolutely love.

  • Commit validation. Prevent a commit if the commit message doesn't reference the branch JIRA. Probably most useful as a toggleable feature.
  • Automatically populate commit message with preconfigured value to eliminate the need to click the button/use hotkey

The basis for this is good. The regrex matching to the branch name is very usefull and can help you with quick setups of commits to make the layout more standard and thus easier to read when reviewing commits.

BUT

  1. my biggest issue is that the regex matching string and the template ARE NOT PROJECT SPECIFIC. So on one project where by branches are named feature/client/TKT-1234_description and on another project where they are named feature/TKT-1234_description I cant use the same capture groups and template because I want one project to template in the customer name but there is no customer name in the other project. These settings should be saved at a project level and imported as a setting.

This allone has made the plugin unuseable for me. If they were to update this I would reconsider the score but as it stands its just too rigid

  1. When making a template where you want to refrence capture groups you cant refrence capture groups by name. This would make it easier when you go to make your template as it allows you to always refrence the correct group no matter how you reorder the regex

3)The regex template needs to be more forgiving. If a capture group is missing just leave the template spot blank, dont just overwrite the template with the entire branch name.

The concept is a good one and could be very usefull so I do hope they get it all fixed up bcause i would love to use a tool like this :)

It’s the only valuable option available for integrating JJ into the IDE. It provides essential features (marking file status in the file tree, showing the changes graph, displaying diffs in the commit panel, and allowing you to commit your changes with a description).

The only complaint I have is that the plugin information sometimes becomes outdated if you interact with JJ outside the IDE, for instance creating a new change (via jj new or via the GG GUI app). For all those that had issues with "Your environment does not support JCEF, cannot use Markdown Editor": this is because AndroidStudio by default uses a runtime that does not support JCEF. Here is how to fix this: Switch your AndroidStudio-Runtime to a version that supports JCEF. Go to "Help" -> "Find Action..." -> "Choose Boot Java Runtime for the IDE". In the field "New" select a runtime that has a version number at least as high as the one that is currently selected but with a description saying "... with JCEF". In my case this was e.g. the third from the top "21.0.7b805 JetBrains Runtime JBR with JCEF (bundled by default)"). Click OK - you will be asked to restart the IDE. That's it!

That being said - this plugin/LLM system still have some way to go. It is kinda buggy. In periods it just hangs or are very slow. It's ability to integrate code correctly is quite bad. I'm mostly write python and I suspect it might be better in languages without significant whitespace.

In a large monorepo the automatic context is basically useless atm. But the interface for including context is ok. I really miss a way making predefined context sets though.. Should be a no-brainer feature imo.

For certain prompts I've gotten better answers from tools like perplexity that combine the model with web-searchers.

The integration with the IDE is quite good, but some of the text-edit boxes behave a bit weird, and there's still some style issues where some text is hard to read due to color choices (using the default theme)

Although it isn't perfect (occasionally using the "apply" button doesn't work and I have to copy and paste the results), this plugin (IntelliJ's PHPStorm) has increased my development speed by a factor of at least 2.

Original review: 12.12.2024 ★★★ I've used this plugin for a couple of months now and even upgraded to Pro recently, but unfortunately Im cancelling my subscription and uninstalling the plugin. When I first installed the plugin it was stable and I found the features and IDE integration much more convenient then web-based AIs. Recently though, its become so unstable that I rarely get to use it. The in-line autocomplete mostly still works as expected, but the UI for asking it questions using context from my project either hangs or throws exceptions. Perhaps in a major version update or two I'll give it a shot again. There's a lot of potential there as long as the stability can be improved.

Update: The Cody team reached out after I posted that review and worked with me to pinpoint the exact issues. Once identified, they went back and implemented fixes and included them in the latest version (7.10.1). I can use Cody again without having it hang or throw exceptions. Thanks guys!

I was hoping this would be better than Copilot, but unfortunately it's not at the moment. It's slower, the auto-complete suggestions are not as good, and the suggestions are displayed with wrong identation which makes it hard to read. I'll give it another go in a few months to see if it improves, but for now I recommend copilot over this.

I've used OrchidE for a couple of years now. It is a great plugin. It is, as far as I'm aware, the single best development environment for Ansible while also making itself one of the best operations environments.

I perform SRE work. I both develop Ansible roles for use in reliability engineering and recovery processes, and use these roles in an operational context. OrchidE handles both tasks beautifully.

Some of my favorite features:

  1. It's highly customizable. While it offers some opinions about how an Ansible project should be structured, I've got a bunch of very weird projects, and it handles them all.
  2. It shows me, inline, the many potential values a variable may have in different inventories, group/host vars, etc. which saves a ton of time sanity-checking how I'm writing a role, flipping between half a dozen files and trying to keep my place in all of them.
  3. Variable autocomplete is a killer feature on its own.
  4. Documentation and autocomplete for hundreds and hundreds of common libraries is insanely useful. I never have to look for third-party docs if I suddenly need to work with another commonly-used role -- it's already in my editor.

Most important of all: it has seriously improved over the last two years as the developer has continued to support it and add features. Two years ago I gave this plugin four stars -- it was a diamond, but still a diamond in the rough. I can safely say this is five stars now: there is simply nothing out there to surpass it.

Indispensable if working with complex ansible projects with multiple groups and roles (e.g. previewing values in different envs is great). Editing encrypted vault files seamlessly is great. Requires careful configuration to work properly though. I have ended up to refactor directory structure to follow "best practice" in some cases to get full benefits of the plugin.

I haven't had any issues with separate yaml files like Kubernetes object definitions or gitlab-ci.yml files.

This is a great plugin, but the issue I found was that it clashed with other yaml files e.g. my Kubernetes manifests, and rendered all those as invalid. I could not find a way to scope it to a single folder or repo.

Anyone who knows how to do this?

I'm sorry to say I have waste so much time on this (suddenly) extremely annoying plugin.

tl;dr: This is a pretty good plugin with some faults. Absolutely worth the price if you regularly work with Ansible, but be ready for some work to get it configured.

Longer review:

If you want the most full-featured Ansible editor with autocomplete, parameter hints, etc. this is awesome. It has some configuration and usability issues which the developer has improved over time but still get in the way of development.

Some general notes:

  1. I'd love it if this could 'detect' when a project looked like an Ansible role and just automatically treat it as one.

  2. When formatting a value into a Jinja template, such as {{ myvar | lower }}, I'd love completions for the filter functions.

  3. The newer method of configuring Ansible folders works well, but the older version was extremely effective for "Ansible-like" projects, where you'd have a couple of playbooks, an inventory, and some roles, without much of the rest of the structure of an Ansible role/stack.

Otherwise, great work. Please keep it up. You save my sanity.
good plugin - but for what it is, it's far too expensive
incredibly expensive for what it is.

This plugin actually works well and performs all functions, but I faced two issues at least:

  1. When I filling up a playbook.yaml file and I try to specify role in roles section it takes a couple of seconds for searching roles in roles directory. This behaviour is a little bit annoying because when I try to list, let's say, five roles I need to spend additional time because for two-four seconds it tries to find role and does nothing.
  2. I cannot use that plugin when Python Template Languages -> Jinja2 included YAML. This breaks the plugin, but the built-in function for writing Jinja2 expressions in some files works very well and I have to disable it for YAML files.

I found this plugin just 'Ok' - helpful at times and unhelpful at others. Pasting yaml into a file would often cause very strange formatting issues (especially with fully qualified task types). Most searching didn't work the way I'd like (others may differ). No inline documentation lookups. However the completion was nice to use and sped my workflow up slightly, but charging nearly a third of what I currently pay for the JetBrains all products pack is so massively disproportionate that I'm going to let this trial lapse sadly. I'd definitely consider purchasing if the price was around £10/year but sadly have to pass - the expense doesn't justify the benefit for me I'm afraid.

Leaving a 5-star review for the simple fact that this app shows as 2-stars when it’s the ONLY actively-developed plugin for working with Ansible and YAML files. It’s also the only one that truly does anything. And while it could use some polishing, it does the job.

My one thing is that our project has a lot of “bad indent” issues. We have some weird nesting structure with playbooks pointing at tasks pointing at tasks. So we’ll have a task file with two spaces, a dash and the “name:”. Orchide wants no spaces, dash name:. I don’t own the project, so I can’t go redoing every single file. It would be nice if this were configurable.

While it has some quirks, it's also day and night compared to literally anything else I could ever find for working with large Ansible projects.

Hope it keeps on steadily improving like it has done overtime.

com.ultrahob.zerolength.plugin.comment:
I just started using this plug-in, but so far it's working pretty well.

While I typically don't want ZWSP and similar characters in my code, there are a few cases where they are very useful, such as in markdown code blocks. For example, where :see_no_evil: would be converted to an emoji by the Hugo site generator even when it's placed inside a code block, inserting a ZWSP between the first colon and the word renders the code correctly. The ZWSP is quite useful in this case.

In Rider 2021.2.2, the configuration can be found at "Settings > Editor > Inspection Settings > Inspection Severity > Other Languages > Potentially confusing code constructs > Zero width unicode character". By default, the severity scope of "In All Scopes" will include warnings in all solution files, including markdown documents. I created a custom scope called ZWSP that excludes markdown files (*.md) and then disabled the "Everywhere else" scope. Now I get ZWSP warnings in all documents except markdown files. Perfect.

I do see one minor issue with the settings label. I believe the word "unicode" is a proper noun, which should be capitalized in English. Also, the term "zero width" should be hyphenated as "zero-width". So, the setting label "Zero width unicode character" should instead read "Zero-width Unicode character".
It just works! And it saved me quite save time. In my opinion it should be a part of default pycharm.
This plugin is fantastic. I had a bizarre issue in my config files due to invisible unicode spaces that had been copied in from a webpage and this plugin was able to find and remove them all.

Any possibility of adding the /u00C2 character identification? In standard UTF-8 encoding, it shows as a whitespace to the naked eye which is not a whitespace. Therefore, unless you turn on show whitespaces and notice that there is that one space which doesn't have the tiny dot identifier, you would never know that it is there. com.visualize-transaction.comment:
参考以下示例

@Service public class OrderService {

@Transactional
public void deleteByOrderIds(List<Long> orderIds) {
    for (Long id : orderIds) {
        deleteOrder(id);
    }
}

@Transactional
public void deleteOrder(Long orderId) {
    // delete order
    // delete order items
}

}

deleteByOrderIds(...) 通过 Spring 代理调用 → ✅ 事务生效 deleteOrder(...) 是 同类内部调用 → ❌ @Transactional 不会单独生效 ✅ 仍然运行在外层事务中 👉 这是一个「预期内、且通常是正确的写法」

插件提示： Same-class @Transactional method call bypasses Spring AOP proxy. The @Transactional annotation on 'deleteOrder' will be ignored. 问题在于： ❌ 暗示这是一个“bug”或“事务失效”， 容易误导开发者认为：整体没有事务，忽略了外层方法已开启事务的上下文

建议优化方向

区分两种情况： 1.外层方法已开启事务 → 提示为 信息级（annotation 冗余，但会加入现有事务） 2.内层方法依赖特殊传播行为（如 REQUIRES_NEW）→ 才提示需要抽取到独立 Service

Spring 트랜잭션 흐름을 시각적으로 확인할 수 있어 디버깅이 훨씬 수월해졌습니다.

사용 환경:
IntelliJ IDEA 2024.1 + Spring Boot 3 + JPA 기반 프로젝트에서 사용했습니다.

장점:

  • 트랜잭션이 시작부터 커밋·롤백까지 어떤 경로로 흐르는지 한눈에 볼 수 있어 코드 이해도가 올라갔습니다.
  • 설정이 거의 필요 없고 설치 후 바로 적용돼서 진입 장벽이 낮았습니다.
  • IDE 반응 속도가 거의 느려지지 않아 실사용에 무리 없었습니다.

추천 대상:
트랜잭션 구조가 복잡하고 디버깅/운영 이슈가 잦은 중형 이상 Spring 기반 서비스 팀에게 강력 추천합니다.
반면에 단순한 CRUD 위주 서비스나 트랜잭션 호출 깊이가 매우 얕은 프로젝트에는 효과 대비 과하게 느껴질 수 있습니다.

총평: ★★★★☆ (4.5/5) — 디버깅 시간을 확실히 줄여줄 유틸리티 플러그인입니다.

csense-idea.kotlin-checked-exceptions.comment:
This plugin is essential for working with Kotlin and interacting with Java code.

However, if there is a runtime exception documented in the Javadoc/Kdoc, it generates an erroneous warning.

This plugin is a life saver when implementing libraries in Kotlin targeting the best Java interoperability. It wrongly warns for unchecked exceptions but still very useful to find out missing @throws annotations. The problem with Kotlin and checked exceptions is, if you don't handle them properly, Java clients have no way to catch them. This plugin lets us find those places where we missed proper exception handling.

I updated cucumberjs_formatter_v3.js with the following code and now it runs

const formatter = function (options) {
  const cucumber = require(options.cucumberLibPath);
  const common = require('./cucumberjs_formatter_common.js');
  //Need to create an instance to see the summary in the console output
  const formatter = new cucumber.Formatter(options);
  const summaryFormatter = new cucumber.SummaryFormatter(options);
  let currentFeature = '';
  let featureIndex = 0;
  /**
   * test-run == Feature == testSuite
   * test-case == Scenario == testSuite
   * test-step == Step == test
   */
  options.eventBroadcaster.on('test-run-started', logFeatureStarted.bind())
  options.eventBroadcaster.on('test-run-finished', logFeatureFinished.bind())
  options.eventBroadcaster.on('test-case-started', logTestCaseStarted.bind())
  options.eventBroadcaster.on('test-case-finished', logTestCaseFinished.bind())
  options.eventBroadcaster.on('test-step-started', logStepStarted.bind())
  options.eventBroadcaster.on('test-step-finished', logStepFinished.bind())

  function logStepStarted(event) {
    const testCaseAttempt = formatter.eventDataCollector.getTestCaseAttempt(event.testCase || event)
    if (testCaseAttempt.pickle.steps[event.index] == null) return;
    const stepName = testCaseAttempt.pickle.steps[event.index].text;
    const stepLine = testCaseAttempt.pickle.steps[event.index].locations[0].line;
    console.log(
        `##teamcity[testStarted name = 'Step: ${common.escape(stepName)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}' captureStandardOutput = 'true' locationHint='file:///${getUri() +
                                                                                                                                                                        ':' +
                                                                                                                                                                        stepLine}']`);
  }

  function logStepFinished(event) {
    const testCaseAttempt = formatter.eventDataCollector.getTestCaseAttempt(event.testCase || event)
    if (testCaseAttempt.pickle.steps[event.index] == null) return;
    const stepName = testCaseAttempt.pickle.steps[event.index].text;
    const result = event.result.status;
    let duration = event.result.duration
    if (duration === undefined) duration = 0
    switch (result) {
      case 'undefined':
        console.log(`##teamcity[testFailed name = 'Step: ${common.escape(stepName)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}' message='' ]`);
        break;
      case 'ambiguous':
      case 'failed':
        console.log(`##teamcity[testFailed name = 'Step: ${common.escape(stepName)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}' details='${common.escape(
            event.result.exception.stack)}' message='' ]`);
        break;
      case 'skipped':
        console.log(`##teamcity[testIgnored name = 'Step: ${common.escape(stepName)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`);
        break;
    }
    console.log(`##teamcity[testFinished name = 'Step: ${common.escape(stepName)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}' duration='${duration}']`);
  }

  function getFeatureName() {
    const length = Object.keys(formatter.eventDataCollector.gherkinDocumentMap).length
    const featureFileName = Object.keys(formatter.eventDataCollector.gherkinDocumentMap)[featureIndex]
    if (formatter.eventDataCollector.gherkinDocumentMap[featureFileName].feature === undefined) return null
    return formatter.eventDataCollector.gherkinDocumentMap[featureFileName].feature.name
  }

  function getUri() {
    return formatter.cwd + '/' + getFeatureFile()
  }

  function getFeatureFile() {
    return common.escape(Object.keys(formatter.eventDataCollector.gherkinDocumentMap)[featureIndex]);
  }

  function logFeatureStarted() {
    //For cases when feature file exists but contains no content
    if (getFeatureName() == null) return;
    if (currentFeature === '') {
      currentFeature = getFeatureName()
      console.log(`##teamcity[enteredTheMatrix timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']\n`)
      console.log(`##teamcity[customProgressStatus testsCategory = 'Scenarios' count = '0' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`)
    }
    console.log(
        `##teamcity[testSuiteStarted name='Feature: ${common.escape(currentFeature)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}' locationHint='file:///${getUri()}']`);
  }

  function logFeatureFinished() {
    console.log(`##teamcity[testSuiteFinished name='Feature: ${common.escape(currentFeature)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`);
    console.log(`##teamcity[customProgressStatus testsCategory = '' count = '0' timestamp = '${common.getCurrentDate()}']`)
    featureIndex++;
  }

  function logTestCaseStarted(event) {
    const testCaseAttempt = formatter.eventDataCollector.getTestCaseAttempt(event);
    const featureName = testCaseAttempt.gherkinDocument.feature.name
    if (featureName !== currentFeature) {
      logFeatureFinished()
      currentFeature = featureName
      logFeatureStarted()
    }
    console.log(`##teamcity[customProgressStatus type = 'testStarted' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`);
    console.log(`##teamcity[testSuiteStarted name='Scenario: ${common.escape(
      testCaseAttempt.pickle.name)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}' locationHint='file:///${getUri() +
                                                                                           ':' +
    event.sourceLocation.line}']`);
  }

  function logTestCaseFinished(event) {
    const testCaseAttempt = formatter.eventDataCollector.getTestCaseAttempt(event.testCase || event)
    const result = testCaseAttempt.result.status;
    switch (result) {
      case 'passed':
        console.log(`##teamcity[customProgressStatus type = 'testFinished' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`)
        break;
      case 'ambiguous':
      case 'failed':
        console.log(`##teamcity[customProgressStatus type = 'testFailed' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`)
        break;
      case 'skipped':
        console.log(`##teamcity[customProgressStatus type = 'testSkipped' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`)
        break;
    }
    console.log(`##teamcity[testSuiteFinished name='Scenario: ${common.escape(testCaseAttempt.pickle.name)}' timestamp='${common.getCurrentDate()}']`);
  }
};

module.exports = formatter

Works well, actively developed and the developer responds within a day. The plugin uses 'vanilla' ansible-lint, so it will (should) behave exactly as expected. But this approach has a few cons:

  • Ansible Lint (just like Ansible) will only tell the line number where the task begins, not where the actual error is
  • Ansible Lint might be slow, which can cause the updates in IDEA UI to be 'laggy'.
  • If Ansible Lint throws and exception, it will not disclose which .yaml file it has issue with, nor which task contains the error that caused linter to crash.

The above limitations are limitations of the ansible linter itself, not the plugin. But I still think it is better to run the 'real thing' instead of trying to reinventing the wheel.

All the hate here is crazy. This plugin is one of my absolute favorite dev tools and I use it almost every day. I guess everyone's mileage varies. For me on Windows with remote interpreter on Homestead, it's magic.

The description of the plug is tragic. No links to documentation. Even though the plugin is only for MacOS, I was able to run it for Linux as well. However, you must use an SSH connection to the server.

Documentation: https://beyondco.de/docs/tinkerwell/getting-started/phpstorm-plugin

An article on how to connect to Docker via SSH: https://dev.to/insolita/how-to-use-invoker-with-docker-containers-59a3

It does work (macOS Mojave, 10.14.6, PhpStorm 2021.2.2), but there are buggy aspects to it. Tips:

  • I generally use it by opening a scratch file.
  • It often seems to be attempting run code that I've commented out. Even adding exit()doesn't always work. It would be handy if that worked. On the other hand, PhpStorm scratch files still have Local History, so you can retrieve stuff you wrote days earlier.
  • You generally won't see error messages unless you use Run With Tinkerwell (T), not Inspect (I) or Show Table (R).
  • Inspect is extremely useful for checking the actual MySQL query that runs and the time it takes. Annoyingly, the text it inserts in the editor window can't be copied and pasted.

I should point out I am using it with the ideaVim plugin which provides Vim keyboard bindings (and for that reason I never really use the standalone app).

Support: I asked the company a question by email (a few days ago) and they haven't replied.

Overall: It's not an insignificant price (over half PhpStorm's annual license subscription) but I am using it regularly.

de.espend.idea.php.toolbox.comment:
It is difficult to overstate how broken and misleading this plugin is in its current state. On the latest stable version of PhpStorm (2025.2.3), PHP Toolbox is completely non-functional. While the IDE reports the plugin as "loaded" in its logs, it fails to provide any of the necessary user-facing components, rendering it entirely useless.

The most egregious issue is the complete absence of a configuration or feedback interface. The author's own README file explicitly directs users to Settings > Languages & Frameworks > PHP Toolbox. This settings panel simply does not exist. There is no tool window, no menu entry, nothing. The plugin installs and then vanishes, leaving the user with a black box. You are expected to create a complex .ide-toolbox.metadata.json file, but are given absolutely zero mechanism to verify if the plugin has parsed it, understood it, or silently choked on an error. The in-editor JSON schema hints are a useless novelty when there is no way to see the result of your configuration.

The problem of usability is compounded by a catastrophic lack of documentation. The official link in the GitHub repository (phpstorm|espend|de/php-toolbox) has been a 404 error for years. This is not a recent issue. My own investigation, using the Web Archive, confirms this link has been dead since at least 2017. The author's parent domain lists their other, actively maintained (and in some cases, paid) plugins, but PHP Toolbox has been scrubbed from existence. The separate "examples" repository is not documentation; it's a collection of context-free snippets that fail to explain the core concepts or demonstrate a practical "before and after" workflow.

It's clear this plugin is abandonware. The GitHub Issues section has seen no meaningful author interaction since 2017. The developer appears to do the bare minimum—bumping the version compatibility number to keep it listed on the marketplace—without performing any actual maintenance or feature development. This is a cynical and deeply unprofessional practice.

In summary, this plugin is a trap. It promises powerful functionality but delivers only frustration. It is undocumented, broken, and unsupported. It actively wastes developers' time and should be removed from the JetBrains Marketplace until it is either properly maintained or officially marked as deprecated. Avoid at all costs.

dev.eltonsandre.kafka.comment:
Pros: It works.

Cons:

Everything is represented as a tree of lists. To get even basic topic information, you must explicitly connect to a topic, which is slow and unnecessary. Basic metadata like partition count, current offsets, and other essential information should be visible directly in the main view (preferably in a table), without having to open or connect to each topic.

Consumer groups and lag are poorly integrated into the UI. Consumer groups are located in a separate branch of the tree, disconnected from topics. There is no clear or practical way to see consumer lag in relation to specific topics or partitions.

Schema Registry is yet another flat list. You can view schema versions, but there is no way to compare them. Without schema diffing or side-by-side comparison, schema evolution is very hard to analyze.

The object tree itself is poorly designed. Search works as simple text highlighting. With thousands of topics, you still have to manually scroll through the list to find slightly highlighted entries. Search should act as a filter — hiding irrelevant items and showing only matching results — not as a visual highlighter.

I didn’t even try data generation. I read that generating and consuming data at the same time is not supported — which is very surprising.

This is my impression after about 10 minutes of use. Barely usable in real-world scenarios. At least there is a trial period before purchase, which is helpful for evaluation.

Overall I liked it, but it needs some improvements. For example: When publishing messages or connecting two topics, the interface freezes waiting for the task to be completed. It would be interesting for the consumer to listen in real time while the producer of fictitious data generates the message. Another point I didn't see was that there's no infinite message generation. Perhaps this is because of the thread that freezes the entire context.

google-java-format.comment: I don’t quite understand the idea behind this code style. It doesn’t look structured: the method name hangs over the arguments, and it’s painful to read. I don’t need a plugin to force code into 80 characters at the cost of increased cognitive load. With the introduction of var, records, and streams, I’d prefer to avoid formatting that involves such trade-offs. My brain is perfectly fine with 100 characters and a few indents that make my neurons click faster. IntelliJ provides extensive support for different code style flavors — try using the built-in tool and configuring your own style. Don’t expect much from Google in this regard; they are outdated.

idea.plugin.protoeditor.comment: For anyone reading this and is also having the frustration of it navigating to the proto file instead of the generated Go stub, I have found that if you put your proto file in its own directory, and then mark that directory as "Excluded", it wont get indexed and navigation will now go to the generated stub file instead of the proto file. Hopefully the developers will put an option in to enable or disable this behavior.
This plugin is useful, however the navigating to protobuf file instead of the generated stub is extremely annoying. The really need an option to disable this. It's aggravating.
It generally works well enough. The most annoying part is that "Go to Declaration or Usages" goes to the .proto file instead of the go implementation with no way of changing the behavior.

Background

In our business scenarios(C++), google protobuf is used in many places, and business protobufs are becoming larger and larger, resulting in the generated code (pb files) also being very large (individual pb files are over 10MB, with 260,000 lines of code).

This causes IDEs to consume a lot of resources when parsing the code generated by protobuf, and for larger projects, it takes about 2 minutes, with memory usage being very high (over 10GB for the entire project). When writing code, code prompts and jumps also appear to be sluggish.

Some Idea

Since this code is automatically generated, is it possible to achieve code prompts and naviagte without generating this code?

Currently, without .pb.cc, .pb.h and other files, there are no code prompts or jumps.
Please consider adding an option to disable jump-to-definition jumping to the .proto file in compiled languages.

Very good code navigation and syntax higlightling in the .proto files. But it captures all ProtoBuf Ctrl + Left-Click navigation in the Java files. So, if you Ctrl + Left-Click on a generated Proto-Class in a Java-File, you can only navigate to the proto declaration, no way to navigate to the generated Java-Code with a Mouse-Click.

Some info for anyone else still having trouble:

If it's not formatting on save, make sure you define a path to the Prettier library on your machine (Language & Frameworks > JavaScript > Prettier > Prettier package field). For me, it would not work if I tried to reference a global installation of Prettier (the path will appear in red text). I had to install it locally in my projects folder (not specifically my project) and then reference that folder (e.g. something like "~/htdocs/utilities/node_modules/prettier").

If it successfully finds Prettier in that folder, the version number will appear next to the path in the package field, and the path will no longer appear red.

Once you've done the above, make sure to tick the "On 'Reformat Code' action" and "On save" tickboxes.

Make sure to also add your desired file formats to the "Run for files" list. For me, I wanted it to format stylesheet files too. This is what my glob pattern looks like:

{**/*,*}.{js,ts,jsx,tsx,scss,css,sass}

Your files should now auto-format on save (may require you to close and reopen the file you're testing in).

I have been using the plugin for about a month and a half now and am very happy with the coding & debugging experience. I switched from VS Code where I had a setup I had been tweaking for years, was very familiar with, so switching to a new editor took me some time to get used to (although I have used JetBrains IDEs a good bit in the past). Once I got past the initial confusion, got my keyboard shortcuts setup properly for the IDE, & settled in I found that using the SFCC B2C plugin has been a joy!

The setup for the plugin is simple and intuitive, and it took me no time at all to get to writing & debugging SFCC code. The plugin has improved my productivity and I would be hard pressed to go back now.

The intentions and syntax highlighting is what makes the development experience so much smoother. I make fewer trips to Dash or my browser to reference documentation, and have to go back fewer times to fix mistakes in my code due. This is due to the superior type recognition and code hints that have been integrated into the editor for each of the file types.

The validation against schema files, property bundles, and XML forms provides many needed details as you code that has made my development experience better. I switch between files less often and stay focused on the file I am editing instead.

The debugger is full featured, and works very well. The Prophet debugger for VSCode has come a long way, and is a great option, but it still has occasional issues. This debugger has been excellent, and feels like an upgrade to me.

The other features of the plugin are what I consider "nice to have" items, but I don't use them often. I use a code build process that uploads code changes as it builds any front-end changes, and cli tools for most tasks for most WEBDav related stuff.

One area that could use improvement for the plugin is the log files view, as it provides no syntax or text wrapping for the files, and they are difficult to scan for information. The loading of the files & file tree also seems to be slow compared to other log viewing options like the Prophet VS Code extension or the Demandware w/Ease Chrome extension, although I haven't done any benchmarking to back that statement up. For me, this is not a big issue as I have keyboard shortcuts setup to use other logging options, but it is worth calling out as I would love for this to be as smoothly integrated as some of the other features.

Overall, using the Salesforce B2C Commerce plugin this has been a great experience. I would love to see more options features added that utilize OCAPI to update meta-data or run jobs, but I have other tools to work with most of these things. For the debugging and coding experience, I have not found another experience that is better. I know that many will balk at the idea of paying for an editor or plugin for an editor, but the price is pretty small, and I am very happy that I took a chance on switching.

Spring 프로젝트의 엔드포인트 관리가 이렇게 편해질 줄 몰랐습니다. Endpoint Lens를 사용하고 나서부터는 일일이 소스 코드를 뒤져가며 매핑 정보를 찾을 필요가 없어졌어요. 직관적인 인터페이스로 전체 구조를 한눈에 파악할 수 있고, 빠른 내비게이션 기능 덕분에 작업 효율이 몰라보게 좋아졌습니다. 특히 서버를 띄우기 전에는 놓치기 쉬운 중복 매핑 이슈를 사전에 잡아주는 세심함에 정말 감동했습니다. 복잡한 프로젝트일수록 진가를 발휘하는 앱이라 주변 동료들에게도 적극적으로 권하고 싶습니다.

Endpoint Lens는 내가 지금까지 사용해본 IntelliJ 플러그인 중 최고라고 말할 수 있습니다! 이 플러그인은 Controller의 API Endpoint를 한 눈에 볼 수 있게 해주는 기능을 제공하는데, 정말 놀라울 정도로 직관적이고 유용합니다. 개발자로서 우리는 종종 프로젝트에서 수많은 API Endpoint를 다뤄야 하는데, 이를 일일이 찾아보는 것은 굉장히 번거롭고 시간이 많이 걸리는 일이었습니다. 하지만 Endpoint Lens 덕분에 이제는 단 몇 초 만에 원하는 Endpoint를 찾을 수 있게 되었죠. 이 플러그인의 가장 큰 장점은 바로 필터링 기능인데요, HTTP Method, Module, Controller 별로 Endpoint를 필터링해서 볼 수 있습니다. 이러한 기능 덕분에 내가 찾고자 하는 Endpoint를 정확하고 빠르게 찾을 수 있었습니다. 또한 Endpoint Lens의 사용자 인터페이스는 매우 직관적이고 깔끔하게 디자인되어 있어서, 처음 사용하는 사람도 쉽게 적응할 수 있을 것 같아요. 마치 IntelliJ에 원래부터 내장되어 있던 기능처럼 자연스럽게 녹아들어 있달까요? 개발자로서 우리에게 시간은 곧 돈이라고 할 수 있는데, Endpoint Lens는 단연코 개발 시간을 크게 단축시켜주는 킬러 플러그인이라고 말씀드리고 싶네요. 앞으로도 계속해서 이 플러그인을 애용할 것 같습니다. Endpoint Lens의 개발자분께 정말 감사드립니다. 당신은 개발자들의 삶의 질을 한 단계 높여주셨어요! 이 플러그인이 널리 알려져서 더 많은 개발자들이 혜택을 받을 수 있기를 진심으로 응원하겠습니다. 정말 수고 많으셨습니다! 🌟*100

Used Postman, Insomnia and Bruno in the past and switched now to jetclient. As with Bruno I can directly place the specific files to a Java Project and have it under version control together with the api project. Even paid for it now because of the possibilities regarding imports/exports of other formats. While I like the possibility to switch "seamlessly" from a REST resource to the API test within one IDE there is always the question how much an additional plugin might influence the IDE and maybe have negative effects on the performance. Also this "seamless" is a bit of a question mark for me regarding the JetClient. Intellij has some command line HTTP Client on board which allows me to navigate from a Request in the Java-Code to generate requests and navigate between them. Right now I have not found out whether this is somehow possibly with JetClient. There is this "API"-tab with which I am playing around now to find out how I can make use of it. And this is another problem with JetClient: The documentation is lacking lot's of information. Certain functionallity is not covered at all but only has an empty page. Don't get me wrong. I think the price is ok. The UI is useful, there are plenty of features. My requirements for rest-api testing with OAUTH2, configuring different environments etc. are covered and easily configured. It just could be more "seamless" and better documented. But I might still consider Integraded HTTP Client and give it a try. A combination of functionality offered by JetClient and HttpClient would be great. :)
Muito obrigado, amei esta versão super leve de uma APIRest Client.
This plugin has made me ditch all Postman for real! Thanks for this!

One of the best API clients I’ve used. The multiple environment selection is a game-changer, allowing me to test across Test/Stage/Prod environments while easily switching between iOS/Android devices. Highly recommend it!

I like the functionality of this plugin. Only a few things are missing for me:

  • I want to save the response even when the request tab is closed. Or some sort of history of the request, like in the Insomnia app;
  • The other one is to see the actual URL of the request. E.g. I want to update the items. The API path should contain the item id, which I extract from the request body in the "Pre-request" section and save it into the variable. But I'm not sure if was it saved or not before the request and there's no option to check the URL of the request I've made.
  • An option to work with folder variables from the higher level. If I have a request in the folder "a/b/c" I want to have the possibility of modifying the variable in the folder "a", not just the current one. Anyway, it's just "nice-to-have" things, even without them this plugin is rocks!
Thanks for this feature, it saves me time and avoids using the Postman software.

io.jmix.studio.comment: Excellent plugin that makes working with Jmix much faster and more convenient. Jmix Studio is intuitive, reliable, and a must-have for productive Jmix development.

No Name Today

A great productivity boost for Jmix developers

This plugin makes working with Jmix much easier and more enjoyable. As a Java developer, I really appreciate having Jmix functionality deeply integrated into IntelliJ IDEA instead of relying on manual configuration and repetitive tasks.
Very easy to use and highly practical, it is a rare and excellent tool as well as platform for Java enterprise full-stack development.

I’ve been using Jmix Studio (and before that, the CUBA platform) across various projects—from government administration software to insurance applications, and even for digital platforms in startups. Jmix Studio has become an essential tool for efficient business application development, allowing for fast progress without sacrificing quality.

One thing to note is that Jmix Studio comes from the same team that created JPA Buddy, a hugely successful plugin with millions of downloads that JetBrains recently acquired and now includes for free with IntelliJ. The maturity of Jmix Studio is evident; the plugin is solid and reliable, with no major issues in recent releases. It provides fantastic productivity boosts through features like boilerplate generation, automated Liquibase migration scripts, and a visual entity modeler—all of which streamline development significantly. After working with Jmix Studio, going back to regular Spring Boot can feel surprisingly limited.

When I was building a digital platform for an eco-startup, Jmix Studio allowed us to get a solution to market quickly for validation—making it perfect for environments where adaptability and speed are key. Whether for large-scale enterprise projects or agile startups, Jmix Studio’s intuitive, integrated setup within IntelliJ helps developers focus on solving core business problems.

In short, Jmix Studio is ideal for those aiming to build scalable, robust applications with minimal friction. It provides productivity, flexibility, and a clear development-to-deployment path, whether you’re in a corporate environment or a fast-moving startup.

Jmix Studio: A Game-Changer for Business Web Application Development

As a business web application developer, Jmix Studio has revolutionized the way I work within IntelliJ IDEA. This plugin is a powerhouse that significantly enhances productivity and streamlines development processes. Here’s why Jmix Studio has become an indispensable tool in my workflow.

Jmix Studio excels in code generation, allowing me to swiftly create DDL and DB migration scripts, UI screens from templates, and essential components like services, listeners, and event handlers. Whether I’m building a new data model or a complete CRUD app over an existing database, Jmix handles it all effortlessly.

One of the standout aspects of Jmix Studio is its per-developer pricing model, which comes without any runtime limitations.

Of course, there is a FREE version of this studio on which you can use the advanced features of Jmix Studio for projects with up to 10 entities (small/meduim projects).

The good thing I can say about about this plugin is that the core functionality mostly works pretty well! 3 solid stars for that.

Now for the not so good things. Code inspections are somewhat broken out of the box, at least in the sense that variables defined with either "*def" or from the "karate-config.js" file won't resolve, creating a huge mess of yellow warnings across the editor when I find myself needing a lot of variables. I'm willing to accept that there might always be things in a Karate project that won't quite jive with how IntelliJ reads code, but this feels a little egregious. Sure, you can hide the warnings, but that's more of a workaround than a solution. I'd like to believe that it's something that could be fixed, either on the side of KarateLabs or on the side of JetBrains depending on where the conflict really is.

  I've also run into some weird behavior during debugging where the test being debugged can't finish a run after stopping at a breakpoint, but I've grown used to it now. Since I'm only using this for API tests, stopping and starting a new run is inexpensive.

io.lmscloud.mdlcode.comment:
I recommend MDLCode for anyone who works with Moodle and wants to keep their code aligned with the platform’s best practices.

It has been very useful in day-to-day development: the plugin helps enforce Moodle’s expected coding standards, reducing rework and providing more confidence before reviews and deliveries. It also offers “wizards” to create Moodle files. I personally do not use this feature, but it is a nice option for those who want to speed up repetitive tasks or are just getting started with the ecosystem.

The main highlight for me is the language string detection: it recognizes calls such as get_string and moodle_exception and warns when a string is missing. This helps avoid common errors and improves internationalization consistency.

Finally, the developer’s website indicates that there are versions for other IDEs, which is a bonus for teams that do not all use the same editor.

===============================

Recomendo o MDLCode para quem trabalha com Moodle e quer manter o código alinhado às práticas da plataforma.

Tem sido bem útil no dia a dia: o plugin ajuda a manter o padrão de código esperado pelo Moodle, reduzindo retrabalho e trazendo mais confiança antes de revisões e entregas. Também oferece “wizards” para criar arquivos do Moodle. Eu particularmente não uso essa parte, mas é uma opção interessante para quem quer acelerar tarefas repetitivas ou está começando no ecossistema.

O destaque, para mim, é a identificação das strings de idioma: ele reconhece chamadas como get_string e moodle_exception e sinaliza quando falta alguma string. Isso ajuda a evitar erros comuns e melhora a consistência da internacionalização.

Por fim, o site do desenvolvedor indica que existem versões para outras IDEs, o que é um bônus para equipes que não usam todas o mesmo editor.

io.recordrelay.plugin.comment: It's been a useful application for me. Great work...

Exactly the kind of tool I've been looking for. On a project with a deep foreign-key tree, pulling a single record into local with all its dependencies was always a pain — one row isn't enough, and between the parents, the children, and getting the insert order right, it always ended in hand-writing SQL. RecordRelay's promise lands right here: pick the root table, enter an ID, and let it walk the FK graph for you — and apparently it catches non-id primary keys and implicit relationships too, which is where most tools fall short. I haven't had the chance to use it heavily yet, but the feature set and the approach look really promising, and having PII masking out of the box is a nice plus. As a first impression, I'd happily recommend it.

RecordRelay solves a problem that many backend developers face every day: reproducing real-world data scenarios without manually copying dozens of related records.

The automatic foreign-key discovery is impressive—it correctly follows dependency chains (including many implicit relationships) and recreates the entire business context in the target database with a single click. The insertion order is handled automatically, eliminating the usual FK constraint headaches.

The built-in PII masking is a standout feature, making it much safer to work with production-derived data in development and staging environments. Field overrides and portable export packages are also extremely useful for sharing reproducible test cases across a team.

I also appreciate that everything happens directly inside IntelliJ. There's no need to switch between SQL clients, write export/import scripts, or manually inspect relationships. The schema explorer and query runner are nice additions that make the plugin even more practical for day-to-day development.

If you regularly debug production issues, prepare test environments, or need to clone complex relational data, RecordRelay can save hours of manual work and significantly reduce mistakes.

Highly recommended for backend developers, QA engineers, and database administrators.

RecordRelay is an incredibly comprehensive and well-thought-out tool. If you frequently need to migrate data from a test database to your local database, this plugin is an absolute game-changer. It handles complex data transfers seamlessly and saves a massive amount of time during development.

What really stands out is how perfectly it integrates as an IntelliJ plugin. The user interface is sleek, highly intuitive, and feels completely native to the IDE, making the whole database syncing process effortless without cluttering your workspace.

A solid 5 out of 5 stars from me! A huge thank you to the publisher, MstrocA, for developing such a fantastic and useful tool. Highly recommended!

The workflow authoring experience is also a game changer, less fat-fingering, easier lookups, and much clearer where values are actually coming from. The idea is very good, tying the code more tightly to the documentation to try and prevent it from going out of date. It will link the documentation directly into the code with a little button at side of relevant code for you to see it.

Price is hidden or obfuscated. That's a red flag warning. If plugin vendors want me to spend time looking at their paid service they need to make a simple entry and state price up front.

If this plugin is improved I shall take another look because it's concept is good. Meanwhile I shall stay with code documentors like PhpDoc and import via Scrivener for excellent LaTeX code booklets.

mdx.js.comment:
It only supports markdown syntax highlighting for top-level markdown. If markdown is a child element, e.g.

<Whatever>
   ## Header
   Lorem ipsum
</Whatever>

it does not receive syntax highlighting.
Very few features (e.g., no structure recognized) Reports many non-existent errors.

Formatting causing unexpected behaviour, can't disable formatting although setting:

Settings -> Editor -> Code Style -> Formatter -> Do not format: *.mdx
causes critical issues in jetbrains RIder. Files in directory tree not loaded after indexing.

Useless stuff. If you have code blocks with (```) for code presentations, like I have, you will get hundreds of errors.

MDX should extend markdown, not restrict it. Very bad. Have anyone at JetBrains tested this stuff? Suppose not.
Won't open some .mdx files! As soon as you disable this plugin, they open again. This is amateur work, I'm baffled.
JetBrains needs to put a lot of work into this MDX plugin. It's extremely outdated and has several annoying broken features.
Frontmatter syntax isn't well supported, most other stuff works just fine
It does not work. The code has no colors, no autocomplete, and no auto-import
Please can we get all markdown features in this plugin too? No tables support in mdx files. No code snippet support...

What works:

  • some imports. Not all
  • some syntax highlight. Not everywhere

What doesn't work:

  • some imports. E.g. 'import Tabs from '@theme/Tabs';' for Docusaurus doesn't work
  • Syntax highlight for Markdown inside HTML tags
  • Search for resource usage (pictures) in *.mdx files via Markdown syntax

As an enhancement and extension of Markdown, I believe that MDX should be built on top of the features of Markdown rather than being a separate branch. Even the simplest code indentation in a code snippet is broken in basic Markdown, making it difficult to understand.

Pros

Really good if you want to work with imports a lot. It provides auto-completion.

Cons

In my case, I wrote blog posts, so I don't need to autocomplete to remind me about those imports because those files don't exist often. They are just tutorials.

This plugin is the only way to work with MDX syntaxis and it works well if you don't use code blocks in it. With code blocks (my case is a ts code) it is broken and a lot of red messages in files are so annoying and they don't help but just disturb.

Of course it's better than nothing, but either it doesn't have a preview option (as for .md files) or this option isn't easy to find it.

In my case this issue reduces the plugin's usefulness to, let's say, 20% or less.

The reason is that I'm not only used to read my own texts but also the text from other people (especially when I fork something from GitHub.)

This does not recognise code blocks. It tries to parse javascript inside code blocks as javascript and formats it according to context outside the block. It shoul evaluate the indentation for inside and outside as separate contexts. The generic markdown plugin works fine for code inside code blocks and even recognises and helps with the correct format. But it breaks when there are jsx attributes in the markdown itself.

This plugin is awesome. Not only the speed is fast, but also can jump across panels. But I found when I jump to some frequent characters like 'e' and '.', the plugin can not show all possible target locations. It would be better if author can fix this bug.

Another hint: right now, when you want to jump to an "m" and because of the number of matches two-char (or even more) jump sequences are needed, one overwrites the other when there are words with consecutive m-characters, e.g., "common".  That is, the key sequence for the first "m" is overridden by the second (only visually).

This problem could be solved easily by building and using a De-Bruijn sequence for the key sequences.  A De-Bruijn sequence has the property that the sequence for n overlaps with the sequence for n+i with the i-th character, e.g., when they overlap, they are equal in the overlapping characters.  Therefore, consecutive characters in the jump key sequences are no problem at all.

Very good, the best I've found for IDEA, although not (yet) as good as avy (kind of a successor of avy-jump) on Emacs. I'm especially missing the functionality of avy-goto-char-timer, see https://github.com/abo-abo/avy#avy-goto-char-timer. That allows you to type while simultaneously highlighting all matches, and after some short idle time it marks all remaining matches with the usual jump target markers. As such, it is equivalent to "jump to char" when you type just one char, but if you type more, it restricts the possible matches drastically which is very handy for jumping to chars occurring frequently like "e", ".", and ",". It would be very cool if that feature could be ported to AceJump-Lite.

me.solohic.gemini-cli-companion.comment:
Overall a genuinely useful plugin that bridges the gap between Gemini CLI and JetBrains IDEs. The open-file context awareness, selection syncing, and native diff view work well and make the terminal-based workflow feel much more connected to your actual editor. For day-to-day use it earns its place.

That said, there are a few friction points that become noticeable pretty quickly when you've spent time with Claude Code or similar tools:

No "copy file reference" shortcut. Claude Code lets you pull a file reference into your prompt with a quick keyboard shortcut directly from the editor. Here you're manually typing paths or relying on whatever context the plugin has already pushed over. A dedicated shortcut or right-click action to insert a file/symbol reference into the active CLI session would be a significant quality-of-life improvement.

Newly created files don't surface as clickable links in the terminal. When Gemini CLI creates a new file, you get the path in text output — but it's not a hyperlink you can click or cmd/ctrl-click to open in the IDE. Claude Code handles this well; newly created files show up as navigable links so you can jump straight to them. Small thing, but it adds up across a session.

The "apply code" flow still runs through the terminal. The diff view is a step in the right direction, but accepting or applying a code change requires interacting with the terminal prompt rather than having a dedicated Apply/Accept button surface directly in the editor at the diff location. An inline IDE-side apply action — similar to how other AI coding tools handle it — would make the review-and-accept loop feel much tighter and less context-switch-heavy.

None of these are dealbreakers, and the core integration is solid. Hoping to see these gaps addressed as the plugin matures.

That being said, there is not a single other plugin i know or ever used that makes new releases with minor changes that often. And each time all users get a notification about this.

I want to share my configuration steps - as I spent some time to understand how to do this.
I use win 7.
1. Download and install Node.js.
2. Use npm coffee-script without -g param. It will install coffee-script to the same directory as Node.
3. Create new "Run/Debug" configuration of "Node JS".
4. Set "Path to Node" to the directory where the node.exe file arranged(C:\Program Files\nodejs).
5. Set "Working Directory" to the path where your coffee script files arranged.
6. Set "Path to Node App JS file" to the "entry point" file of your project or any file which you want to run.
7. Check "Run with CoffeeScript plugin" checkbox.
8. Set "Path to cofee executable" to the cofee-script module( In my case C:\Program Files (x86)\nodejs\node_modules\coffee-script\bin\coffee). This file will contain next code

How about seeing what went wrong? I have a coffee file run with node.js and all I can see is some stack trace (but it can't find the fs.js file so no sources). No error message, no error in the console (as I used to have on linux terminal), nothing. How figure it out? ;)

I'm on OSX and generating previews of compiled coffeescript is incredibly CPU-intensive - is there possibly a bug here? It doesn't seem to be handing the file off to coffee -c, which is what I would expect.

Finally figured out how to use it.
I'm pretty sure that there must be an easier way, but this worked for us:

1. install the NodeJS plugin, and npm coffee-script.
2. of the Run/Debug configurator.
3. set 'Path to Node' to the location of node (e.g. on OSX: /usr/local/bin/node).
4. set 'Path to Node App JS File' to the location of coffee (eg /usr/local/bin/coffee).
5. set "application parameters" to your .coffee file (eg test.coffee)

The key thing is to run coffee from node. If you look in the coffee file, you'll see that it's a nodejs file with the node shebang.

Unfortunately, the plugin is not reliably usable in my project.

It fails to correctly resolve required_providers when they are defined in a separate file, which is a common and recommended practice in Terraform projects. Even though the providers are properly declared, the editor reports that the provider is not installed.

When executing the suggested quick-fix action, the plugin generates an additional required_providers block — but in the wrong file. This results in redundant or incorrect configuration instead of resolving the actual issue.

In its current state, the plugin is not practically usable for properly structured Terraform projects.

Das Plugin ist in meinem Projekt leider nicht zuverlässig nutzbar.

Es ist nicht in der Lage, die required_providers korrekt aufzulösen, wenn diese in einer separaten Datei definiert sind (was bei Terraform-Projekten ein gängiges Vorgehen ist). Obwohl die Provider ordnungsgemäß deklariert sind, zeigt der Editor an, dass der entsprechende Provider nicht installiert sei.

Führt man die vorgeschlagene Quick-Fix-Aktion aus, wird ein zusätzlicher required_providers-Block generiert – jedoch im falschen File. Dadurch entstehen redundante oder inkorrekte Konfigurationen, statt das eigentliche Problem zu lösen.

In diesem Zustand ist das Plugin für strukturierte Terraform-Projekte leider nicht praktikabel einsetzbar.

As already mentined, re-indexing is a problem. There are also incorrect validations like that "id" is a required field for the import block (it isn't with the "identity" usage) Another quite huge problem is the run confguration. This one is bound to the parent folder name, so if I'm in a different folder, the same run configuration is re-used. e.g., "/mypath/terraform" vs "/myotherpath/terraform", if I execute terraform in the first one, the same run configuration is re-used for the second one, meaning if I'm in the second path and run Terraform via the play button in the configs, the run config of the first path is executed, so this folder is completely ignored. This means, that I always have to delete the run configs if I want to make use of the run button in another path (with the same folder name at the end)
The plugin is very useful, but It has a lot of syntax/reference checks problems. For example, it marks all my variables as unused (so that I may delete them), but It's not true.
Plugin itself works alright, but it continuously fails to re-index if any dependencies are updated, greatly reducing its usefulness if you frequently update your dependencies(as you should).

I put this in a recent 'Submit Feedback' report, but felt it necessary to also post here.

JetBrains has set such a high bar of quality for their other products and plugins, that the continuously poor user experience of the Terraform plugin is shocking and confounding. It's better than nothing, but not by much.

It feels to me that no one at JetBrains actually uses Terraform / OpenTofu / Terragrunt in any meaningful way - as any DevOps/SRE/Cloud practitioner who uses and relies upon these tools for their work, day in and day out would.

What appear to be completely obvious and common bugs - just read the other Terraform Plugin Reviews - take considerable amount of time to even be noticed by the JetBrains team, and we users struggle to give the IDE developers reproducible environments for every single bug/issue discovered and reported, but it's not enough. The team has made minor incremental improvements since taking it over from the original author (Vlad), but continues to miss the painfully obvious issues.

I love JetBrains IDE's for nearly everything else - Java, Go, PyCharm, JS/TS, YAML, Kubernetes... but somehow JetBrains continues to fail miserably at the Terraform plugin, and seemingly cannot figure out what Terraform is, who uses it or how it's used. It honestly makes me a bit sad.

for people experiencing .md files looking like text only, here is a possible fix (worked for me):

  • Go to Settings | Editor | File Types.
  • Search for a type named "Markdown document generated by AI tools".
  • If you see *.md inside that list, remove it.
  • Then, go to the standard Markdown file type in that same list and add *.md back to it.

This plugin would be about 5x better for new users with some instructions of what's possible. Here, let me help.

  • Create an extension for your templates. If they are HTML, *.gohtml is already defined for you.
  • Settings | Editor | File Types has the place to add your template type. The hidden gem: once started, there is a popup for the type of the underlying template. So I created *.goyaml and then told it these underlying type of the file was YAML. Voila, language sensitive rendering.
  • Learn how to use gotype annotations on your templates: https://blog.jetbrains.com/go/2018/12/14/go-templates-made-easy/. Of course that's a Jetbrains blog, so it doesn't actually tell you what those annotations are. They basically are the cue for the editor to tell what kind of object is at the root of the instance hierarchy provided at the template.Template.Execute call. Voila, template source objects are context-aware.

Now you can actually get some work done. w00t w00t!

Works ok, but as another commenter mentioned, it's a problem for Hugo templates, which have a .html file extension. On the other hand, the Angular plugin manages to get HTML syntax highlighting working on .html files without having to reassign file types, so it is apparently possible, though I assume this is done by detecting the project type via some sort of heuristic. Alternately a simple solution would be to  offer a per-project setting, e.g. a checkbox "Treat .html files as Go templates".
